title: UCL engineering students designed a bamboo cargo trike for Ethiopian farmers
body_html:
Context

Across three consecutive years — 2016, 2017 and 2018 — Master's students in UCL's Department of Mechanical Engineering ran live engineering design projects with Bamboo Bicycle Club, each cohort building on the last. Real briefs, real prototypes, supervised within the department.

What we did

We set students a genuine design-for-development challenge: build a load-carrying bamboo bike that could work in a low-resource setting. One project, "Pedal Progress" — supervised by Dr Eral Bele — focused on Ethiopia, chosen for its large agricultural sector and its bamboo forests. The brief was to fill the gap between carrying goods by hand and using a motorised vehicle: a cargo bike that is durable, simple to build, affordable, and low in environmental impact.

Verified outcome

The Pedal Progress prototype was a rear-loading bamboo tricycle with:

  • a 150kg cargo capacity
  • hemp-resin joints
  • seven-speed gearing with a rear differential
  • an expected lifespan of around five years
  • a lower carbon footprint than an equivalent steel bike

A later UCL cohort developed an electric version, adding an integrated battery, a rear-hub motor and a weatherproof cargo box.

Quote

No participant quote is verified for this project, so we make none up. The work speaks for itself: a working prototype, designed and tested by Master's engineers against a real Ethiopian farming brief.

Why it matters

It is one of the clearest examples of Bamboo Bicycle Club as a design-for-development partner, not just a bike kit. Real students, a real country brief, and a real prototype — bamboo applied to a genuine mobility problem.
